title.en: Long and short vowels, s, j — and weak endings

explanation.short: A vowel before one consonant, or at the end of a word, is long: gut is GOOT. Before two consonants it is short: bitte is BIT-uh. s before a vowel buzzes like English z (sie is ZEE) and j is English y (ja is YAH). An -e at the end of a word is a faint "uh" (bitte), and so is -er (Lehrer is LAY-ruh).
explanation.more: Count the consonant letters after the strong vowel: none or one means long (der, zu, war, wir, Vater, sagen); two, or a doubled letter, means short (Wasser, Mann, kommen, nicht, richtig). Small words are exceptions and stay short: in, mit, an, das, was, ist, bin, hat, es. A few other words break the pattern too (Buch has a long u). s is a plain hiss at the end of a word or before a consonant: Haus, ist. The faint endings are the same in Name (NAH-muh), aber (AH-buh) and Vater (FAH-tuh). This is a guide, not a law: German has exceptions, so listen as you read.

options: short i, faint "uh" at the end: BIT-uh
long ee, clear "eh" at the end: BEE-teh

checks.prompt: How is the "a" in "Wasser" said? (two s's follow it)
